phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on short alpha — the name expires outward, like a breath seen in cold air.
Delta plus long eta, the long vowel that opens the name into the unseen.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-dace' — the first syllable is pitched high and sharp; the second is long and level, like the floor of the underworld.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *ǵʰew-, 'to see' — the same root gives Greek οἶδα (oida), 'I know'

pronunciation.note: Hádēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἅιδης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name literally means 'the Unseen,' and the acute on the first syllable gives it the force of a warning.

domains.title: The Unseen King
domains.subtitle: The Dead, Wealth, and the Underworld
domains.lead: Hádēs is not evil; he is the necessary guardian of the dead. His realm is not hell but the place beneath the earth where all souls go — good and bad alike. He is also Plouton, the wealthy one, because the earth holds grain, metals, and the buried dead.

cards.name: The Underworld
cards.desc: Not a place of torment but the common destination of all mortals, ruled with strict impartiality.

cards.name: Wealth of the Earth
cards.desc: As Plouton he owns gold, silver, and the fertility that rises from below.

cards.name: The House of Hádēs
cards.desc: A place of shadow, gates, and the three-headed dog Kerberos who allows entry but not exit.

cards.name: Immovable Justice
cards.desc: Unlike other gods, Hádēs almost never intervenes in human affairs; his realm is governed by law.

symbols.name: Cornucopia

mythology.lead: Hádēs appears rarely in Greek myth because his realm is separate from the world of the living. His most important myth is the abduction of Persephonē, which explains the seasons and establishes his connection to Demeter.

myths.title: The Rape of Persephonē
myths.text: With Zeús's permission, Hádēs burst from the earth in a golden chariot and seized Persephonē while she gathered flowers in a meadow. Demeter's grief caused famine and winter until Zeús negotiated a compromise: Persephonē spends part of the year above with her mother and part below with her husband. This is the Greek explanation for the seasons — life and death take turns because even gods must share.

myths.title: The Judges of the Dead
myths.text: In the underworld, the dead are judged by Minos, Aiakos, and Rhadamanthys — three former mortals made just. The wicked go to Tartaros, the ordinary dead to the fields of Asphodel, and the heroic few to Elysium. Hádēs presides over this system without passion; his justice is administrative, not punitive.

myths.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
myths.text: Orpheus descended to Hádēs's realm to retrieve his dead wife Eurydice. His music moved even the underworld king, who allowed her to follow on the condition that Orpheus not look back. At the threshold of the upper world, Orpheus looked, and she was lost. The myth shows Hádēs as capable of pity but bound by the law of his realm.

myths.title: The Cap of Darkness
myths.text: The Cyclopes gave Hádēs a helmet that made the wearer invisible. He lent it to Athena in the Gigantomachy and to Perseus for his mission against Medousa. The cap is the material form of his nature: Hádēs is the unseen, and his power is to make others unseen as well.

lore.syncretism: The Romans called him Pluto or Dis Pater, emphasizing his wealth rather than his dread. In mystery cults — especially the Eleusinian Mysteries — he and Persephonē were central figures who promised initiates a better afterlife. Christian writers later used Hades as a name for the underworld itself and, in the New Testament, as a temporary abode of the dead. The name passed into English as the word for the realm of the dead, though the Greek god is morally neutral.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hádēs remains the archetype of the underworld ruler in Western imagination. Unlike the Christian devil, he is neither tempter nor torturer; he is the strict, fair administrator of death. The Eleusinian Mysteries, which honored Demeter and Persephonē, were among the most important religious institutions of the ancient Mediterranean and influenced later ideas of salvation. In modern fantasy, Hades appears in countless adaptations, usually darker than his Greek original. Restoring Hádēs restores the name of the god who receives everyone in the end.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hádēs is the god we do not want to meet. Not because he is cruel, but because meeting him means the story is over. He is the final impartiality: rich and poor, hero and coward, all pass through his gates. The Greeks found this terrifying but also just. There is no favoritism in death.

In a culture that often denies death, Hádēs is a corrective. He does not threaten; he waits. The restoration of his name in Unicode is a small acknowledgment that the Greeks had a vocabulary for the end of life that was neither sentimental nor despairing — simply true.
lore.archaeology: Eleusis preserves the Telesterion and the Ploutonion, the cave from which Hades was said to have emerged to seize Persephone. The Nekromanteion at Ephyra on the Acheron was an oracle of the dead visited by Odysseus in the Nekyia. In Asia Minor, the Ploutonion at Hierapolis (Pamukkale) emitted suffocating gases and was enclosed as a sanctuary of Pluto. Votive reliefs from Locri Epizephyrii and Athens show the god with Cerberus and Persephone.
